`docs/HIVE.md`:

```md
# The hive: an AI analyst team on top of ReverseAI

The hive is an optional team of AI agents that analyses a native program with ReverseAI and
rebuilds it as C or C++ source. A **queen** splits the work, a **hive of bees** works in parallel, and
an **independent council** plus a deterministic **evidence checker** decide what is accepted.
The ReverseAI engine itself stays model-free: the hive is a separate layer in `hive/` that
talks to the engine only through its MCP server and command line.

Status: experimental. This guide describes the integrated 0.9.0 hive; it needs prepared Ghidra
exports (`reverseai prepare`).
The default path uses your Claude Code subscription, or your Codex login for Codex bees.
An explicitly configured self-hosted server is an alternative (see [Self-hosted models](#self-hosted-models-experimental));
the agent CLIs and the queen's checks still apply.

## Roles

| Role | Who | Does | Never does |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Queen | Python code (`hive/queen.py`) | Exports the program map, freezes the plan, schedules bees, compiles and links, runs the checks, computes the verdict | Write code, review, vote, or override a check |
| Planner | One bee per bounded group, plus interface reconciliation when needed | Proposes modules, evidence-backed skips and declarations; the queen validates and freezes the interface | Rebuild or judge |
| Builder | One bee per module, in parallel | Rebuilds its module's functions as C from the evidence; writes claims citing finding IDs | Edit the contract or another module |
| Councillor | Three per module, one lens each | Tries to refute the module against the original's assembly: control flow and arithmetic, input/output, data and memory | Write anything; see the author's notes |
| Tester | One bee, only with `--run-original` | Designs conformance cases from strings and logic | Run anything |

## How a run works

1. **Survey.** The queen prepares the file once (Ghidra analyses it in its locked container and
   keeps the project in the private cache), then exports every function, call and string into
   `survey/map.json`.
2. **Pre-flight.** Before any bee is spent, the queen checks whether the program is packed or
   obfuscated (see [Pre-flight](#pre-flight)). A packed program stops the run with the reasons,
   unless you start it with `--allow-packed`. Then the queen chooses the language: C, or C++ when
   the map shows C++ (see [Languages](#languages)).
3. **Plan.** Phase A partitions the map deterministically. In phase B, planners propose modules
   and declarations from bounded groups; interface tasks reconcile conflicting declarations. The queen
   checks exact function coverage and evidence-backed skips, splits oversized modules, checks that
   the assembled contract compiles on its own, and freezes it read-only (see [Group planning](#group-planning-phases-a-and-b)).
   Configured self-hosted targets must pass their [capability checks](#automatic-capability-checks) first.
4. **Build.** Builders work in parallel, one folder each. Every module is compiled alone from a
   clean stage containing snapshots of its source and the frozen contract, with
   `-Wall -Wextra -fwrapv -fno-strict-aliasing`. This requires Clang with a closed virtual
   filesystem (`-ivfsoverlay`, no fallthrough): generated includes and include-existence queries
   can see only that stage and the compiler's system header directories. Other compilers are
   refused. Before the planner starts, a native positive/negative probe checks the selected
   compiler once: the outside-file query must fail and nonempty inline assembly must be disabled
   in the selected C or C++ mode. The compiler receives `-fno-gnu-inline-asm` and `-fno-asm-blocks`;
   the preprocessor VFS alone does not confine the assembler. Symlinked or hard-linked sources
   and contracts are refused. The queen scans the whole expanded output for file-loading
   constructs, without trusting source line markers, then compiles the original source in the
   same confinement so macro context is kept. Generated source-location overrides are refused.
   Each compiler command has a 60-second deadline and captured-output limits of 16 MiB stdout
   and 256 KiB stderr; crossing a limit stops the command (the owned process group on POSIX).
   Compiler messages go back to the builder, at most three times. A builder must report every
   assigned function rebuilt and status `done`; repair reports update the entries they touch
   while preserving the other functions' reported state.
5. **Council.** Three councillors, each with a fresh context, review a renamed copy of the module
   without the builder's notes. Only behavioural differences with evidence (an address in the
   original or a finding ID) count. The builder must fix them or disprove them with evidence; a
   fresh council reviews again. A module still refuted after two rounds is **disputed**, never
   silently accepted. Every configured seat must return a valid verdict; a missing or failed
   seat leaves the module **incomplete**, including a refused Codex seat in a mixed council.
6. **Link.** The queen links all modules and routes undefined or duplicate symbols to the module
   that owns them, at most three rounds. Each repaired module returns to council on its new
   source; a missing or refuting verdict prevents acceptance.
7. **Evidence check.** `tools/hive_check.py` re-runs every question that a claim cites, through
   ReverseAI itself, and keeps a claim only if each cited finding ID comes back with a
   `supported` or `derived` verdict. Finding IDs are bound to the file's hash and the result's
   content, so a made-up ID, an ID from another file or a stale ID is rejected. The queen binds
   every citation to the target file and requires the checker's input hash to match the survey.
   These checks run after the last repair, including behaviour repairs.
8. **Behaviour (optional).** With `--run-original`, the tester writes cases; the queen runs the
   original and the rebuild on each case in a fresh folder and compares the exit code, stdout and
   every file created (by hash), and stderr with the program's path masked (its first 2,000
   characters). At least **two nonempty cases**, with unique IDs after filename
   normalisation, must complete; empty suites, colliding IDs and timeouts cannot prove behaviour.
   Differences go to one fixer bee, at most two rounds; changed modules return to council.
   A failed relink removes the older binary, invalidates the link result and stops the behaviour
   proof; the queen never falls back to a binary built from earlier objects.
9. **Verdict.** Code computes it: **accepted** only if the program links, every module is
   accepted by its council, no function is a stub, the checker rejected no claim and every
   conformance case is identical. Without `--run-original` the best verdict is
   **accepted without behaviour proof**.

With `--run-original --fuzz N`, add up to 500 deterministic mutants after the ordinary behaviour
checks and repairs (`N` defaults to 0, off). They change only case-file bytes, including stdin files,
using bit flips, insertion, deletion, truncation, boundary bytes and splicing between cases; arguments
stay unchanged and each file stays within the 64 KiB case limit. The input SHA-256 and source case ID
seed each sequence. Mutants use the final rebuilt binary and extend the conformance totals; differences
are reported without another repair round. No-op and duplicate inputs are discarded with bounded
attempts; cases whose files the executor skips add no mutants. Complete mutant pairs are compared
even if others time out or are missing: the report keeps the plain result, differing cases and a
separate `incomplete` list. Any incomplete mutant prevents acceptance. `tests/fuzz.json` records the
seed and bounded base64 inputs of both differing and incomplete mutants for reproduction, and is
cleared at the start of each conformance attempt.

## Group planning: phases A and B

Phase A is implemented in `hive/partition.py`: it splits the map deterministically into
bounded groups while keeping every function exactly once. Functions that call each other,
share strings or touch the same data tend to stay together, but count and byte caps take
precedence. Calls across groups remain explicit. A singleton that is still too large keeps
an inline sample plus complete overflow side files with hashes and counts; unattached rows
are retained too. The global summary declares its omissions and cannot prove coverage.

The queen uses phase B in `hive/planning.py` to propose a plan from those groups. Each planner receives
only its own `map.json`, a bounded `summary.json` and an `interfaces.json` index. Large inputs
are paged inside that group's readable folder; every page has a count and SHA-256, and no
individual page exceeds `max_prompt_bytes`. The same limit bounds the combined task and
initial map/summary/index bytes. It does not measure the agent CLI's system prompt, tool
definitions or total token context. An indivisible record above the cap stops planning
with `planning_payload_too_large`, rather than being silently truncated.

Every group function must be assigned or skipped with a reason and evidence. The queen's
planning code checks exact coverage, shared declarations, dependencies and global owners.
Conflicting declarations get a bounded interface task that can select only an existing
variant. Unknown layouts or unresolved conflicts stop the plan; opaque types cross module
interfaces only through pointers/references. Final modules use `m01`, `m02`, etc., separately
from partition groups `g0001`, `g0002`, etc. A global definition belongs to the module that
contains its `owner_entry`, including after a large module is split.

The output is `plan/manifest.json`, `plan/interfaces.json` and `plan/contract.h` (or `.hpp`).
The manifest binds input, map, partition, planning policy, declarations and assignments by
hash. `validate_bundle` rechecks those bindings without a planner. Partial verified proposals
and interface decisions can be resumed from `plan/progress.json`; prior failed attempts
remain in the queen's history. The queen compiles and freezes the contract before builders
start. Planning alone does not accept a module or prove that the rebuild behaves like the original.

If a group fails or is refused before the plan is frozen, resume validates the saved progress
and retains completed groups and interface decisions. Only unfinished work is planned again;
[refusal recovery](#explicit-local-recovery-after-a-refusal) requires explicit local consent.
Once frozen, the verified plan is reused without another planner. The integrated tests use
simulated agent processes and servers; they do not demonstrate a complete curl reconstruction
or measure a whole run on a local model.

## Who has the final word

- A failed check cannot be overruled by any agent. The council can only add a veto.
- The queen is code. She cannot vote, and her plan is reviewed only through its results.
- A claim without a resolvable citation is dropped, whatever it says.

## Speed

- **One MCP server per bee.** ReverseAI's MCP server answers one request at a time, so the hive
  gives every bee its own server process: Ghidra questions from different bees run in parallel
  containers instead of queueing.
- **Analyse once.** Preparation runs Ghidra's auto-analysis once; later questions load the
  cached project.
- **Barriers only where needed.** Modules run as independent pipelines (build, compile, council,
  repair); the queen waits only after the plan, before linking and before the final checks.
- `--bees N` sets how many bees work at once (default 4). Each contained Ghidra question uses up
  to 2 CPUs and 2 GiB, so size N to your Docker VM. `--max-bees` caps the whole run.

## Pre-flight

Rebuilding a packed program from static evidence only rebuilds its unpacking stub, and
obfuscation (flattened control flow, virtual machines) defeats decompilation, so the queen checks
first, deterministically, in `hive/preflight.py`:

- packer section names (UPX, MPRESS, ASPack, PECompact, Themida, VMProtect, Enigma, NsPack, ...)
  and packer marker strings in the file;
- byte entropy of each executable segment and of the whole file, computed from the approved file
  over the segment ranges that ReverseAI verifies (compressed or encrypted bytes are close to
  8 bits per byte);
- imports that only load more code (`LoadLibrary`/`GetProcAddress`, `dlopen`/`dlsym`, ...);
- very few functions or strings for the code size, or one function holding most of the code.

Any strong signal gives **packed** (the run stops); two weak signals give **suspected** (the run
warns and continues). The result is in `survey/preflight/preflight.json` and in the report.
Nothing is unpacked or executed: unpacking stays your decision. A clean verdict does not prove
that a program is neither packed nor obfuscated.

## Languages

`--language auto` (the default) rebuilds in C, or in C++ when the map shows at least two signs of
C++: mangled names (`_Z...`), qualified names (`Class::method`), C++ runtime imports
(`__cxa_throw`, `__gxx_personality_v0`, ...) or `operator new`/`delete`. `--language c` and
`--language cpp` force a choice. C++ builders rebuild classes with the layout the assembly shows,
pinned with `static_assert`, and virtual methods in vtable order; the contract becomes
`contract.hpp` and the queen compiles with `c++ -std=gnu++17`. Other languages (Java for Android
apps, ports to Rust, Go or Python) are not handled yet.

## Bee models

`--bee-policy claude` (the default) runs every bee on Claude Code. `--bee-policy codex` runs every
bee on the Codex CLI (`codex exec`), and `--bee-policy mixed` alternates: odd-numbered modules are
built by Claude and even ones by Codex, repairs stay with the module's builder, and each council
gives two of its three seats to the other client. The planner, the tester and the behaviour
fixer stay on Claude. These flags select agent clients; each user chooses the models behind them.
Every council seat still needs a fresh context independent of the author. Running Claude and
Codex against the same local model does not establish model diversity.

Each attempt records `provenance.client`, the requested model, any observed model/digest, a
context ID and `origin` (`primary` or `fallback`). `provenance.server_kind` distinguishes
`cloud` (the default provider path), `local` (a configured loopback server) and `remote` (a
configured non-loopback server). These describe routing, not where a server ultimately performs
inference. Unknown observed identities stay null. The per-module `model_diversity` result is
true/false only when all relevant author/reviewer identities are observed; otherwise it is null.
Client names and requested model aliases alone do not prove diversity.

Codex bees are less fenced than Claude bees, and this was measured on 2026-10-31 with
codex-cli 0.165.0 on macOS: writes outside the bee's folder were denied, but a Codex bee could read
files elsewhere on the disk, run programs (including the input), and reach the network from inside
`codex exec` in both its read-only and workspace-write modes, although `codex sandbox` alone blocks
it. The hive therefore probes the Codex sandbox before its first Codex bee and refuses Codex bees
while the probe reaches the network. `--codex-allow-network` skips that refusal for operators who
accept the risk on software they would run anyway; never use Codex bees on malware.

## Configure your own model

Hive is independent of a particular model. Choose a model and server that support all three:

- **Tools:** a native tool call, its result, and a following answer through the selected agent CLI.
- **Structured output:** a JSON instance conforming to Hive's schema through Claude Code's
  `--json-schema` or Codex's `--output-schema` path. Returning the schema itself, a wrapper or
  prose containing JSON is insufficient.
- **Active context:** at least `--required-context` tokens (default **65536**). Allow space for
  the CLI's system prompt, tools, evidence, history and output. The planning byte cap is separate
  from token context, and this minimum does not guarantee completion of a particular program.

Install/configure the agent CLIs and prepare your chosen server and model before invoking Hive.
Configured fallback clients must also be installed before startup. Hive's routing flags do not
install a server, download a model or start a server process.

### Self-hosted models (experimental)

`--model-server URL` selects a primary server. Claude bees need Anthropic Messages support and
`--model NAME`; Codex bees need OpenAI Responses support and `--codex-model NAME`. Mixed policy
needs both names and both API paths. A Chat Completions endpoint alone is insufficient. Pass the
server root URL without `/v1`: Claude uses that base; Codex appends `/v1` for Responses.

The primary must be on loopback unless you add `--model-server-remote`, explicitly consenting to
send prompts and program evidence to another machine. This consent does not authorize a remote
fallback. Loopback addresses also do not prove that a server performs inference locally.

The bees retain their CLI, role tools and checks: Claude uses folder-scoped writes and `dontAsk`;
Codex keeps its sandbox and isolation probe. Self-hosted bees receive an allowlisted environment
(system basics, locale and certificate paths) and routing, with a placeholder token for Claude.
Subscription logins, cloud credentials and API/repository tokens are excluded.

### Server settings

Set these on the server process or its service, then verify the **active** configuration. Select
parallelism against available memory and measure latency before increasing Hive's `--bees`.
A longer context and more concurrent requests consume more memory; no machine-size or throughput
estimate is implied by these examples.

| Setting | Ollama | vLLM |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Listen locally | `OLLAMA_HOST=127.0.0.1:11434` | `--host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000` |
| Context | `OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=65536`; inspect `ollama ps` and `/api/ps` for the chosen loaded model | `--max-model-len 65536` bounds prompt plus output; the model and available memory must support it |
| Parallelism | Start with `OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=1`; coordinate it with Hive's `--bees` | `--max-num-seqs` bounds sequences per iteration; start small and coordinate it with Hive's `--bees` |
| Tools | Choose a model/API path supporting tool calls and tool results | Configure `--enable-auto-tool-choice`, a `--tool-call-parser` for the chosen model and a tool-compatible chat template; set `--chat-template` if needed |
| Structured output | Schema support must work through the selected Messages/Responses client, beyond native `/api/chat`'s `format` option | Structured outputs default to backend `auto`; `--structured-outputs-config.backend` selects it explicitly. Verify the required API/client path, not just Chat Completions |

For a manually managed Ollama server, an example in a separate terminal is:

```sh
OLLAMA_HOST=127.0.0.1:11434 OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=65536 OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=1 ollama serve
```

If Ollama already runs as an app or service, configure and restart that instance instead. Use
an already installed model name in the Hive command, from another terminal:

```sh
python3 -m hive run --inputs /path/to/approved-inputs --file program --out new-hive-run \
  --model-server http://127.0.0.1:11434 --model your-installed-model \
  --required-context 65536 --max-tool-rejections 8 --bees 1
```

Ollama settings and diagnostics: [context length](https://docs.ollama.com/context-length),
[server configuration and concurrency](https://docs.ollama.com/faq),
[structured outputs](https://docs.ollama.com/capabilities/structured-outputs),
[loaded-model metadata](https://docs.ollama.com/api/ps).
vLLM settings: [serve options](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/cli/serve/),
[tool calling](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/features/tool_calling/),
[structured outputs](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/features/structured_outputs/).
Use the documentation and help matching your installed server version.

### Active context metadata

Hive reads the configured model's serving context from Ollama-compatible `/api/ps`
(`context_length`). When that API is absent or unrecognized, it tries vLLM-compatible
`/v1/models` (`max_model_len`). The model name or ID must match the configured name
exactly, and the reported length must be a positive integer. Recognized metadata with
a missing model or invalid length stays unknown; Hive does not borrow another model's
limit or replace a loaded context with a larger limit from another API.

If no recognized source provides usable metadata, `context` is `unsupported`:
**“Active context is not verifiable on this server”**, or *non verificabile su questo
server*. This differs from a measured context below `--required-context`, which is an
`error`. Connection, authentication and other metadata-query failures are also errors.
Expose the chosen model's serving metadata and verify the server's active settings.
The Python `selfhost.check_model` API can accept a `context_query(server, model)` reader
for another server API; the CLI has no flag to inject one.

### Automatic capability checks

Before planning or workers, Hive checks every configured self-hosted primary and authorized
fallback target, once per client, including fallback targets not yet activated. The default
cloud path, with no `--model-server`, keeps its existing behavior without these capability probes.
A configured local fallback is still checked when the primary uses cloud.

One short process through the actual selected CLI reads a random nonce with a tool,
calls ReverseAI's real MCP `export_function` on a function from the input survey, and
returns the nonce under a small output schema. It uses the same ReverseAI MCP server,
input directory and tool configuration as the bees. `mcp_tool` is `ok` only when native
CLI events show that the server accepted the call with arguments matching that surveyed
file and function; the model's story or final JSON cannot establish acceptance.
A surveyed function, configured MCP tools and an accepted native result are required.

Read, MCP and structured output share that one capability process, counted as
`network_probe` in the start budget. Codex may first need a separate isolation probe,
also counted. Hive separately compares the server's declared **active** context with
`--required-context`. These checks do not measure effective context retention, peak
memory, inference speed or whether a long reconstruction will succeed.

`.hive/model-checks.json` records `tool_roundtrip`, `mcp_tool`, `structured_output` and
`context`, each with status `ok`, `unsupported` or `error`, a message and a configuration
suggestion. All must be `ok`:

| Result | Meaning and action |
| --- | --- |
| `ok` | This small capability check passed; normal compiler, council, evidence and behavior checks remain required. |
| `unsupported` | A capability was not demonstrated. For `mcp_tool`, provide a surveyed function, the configured MCP tools and accepted native tool evidence. For `context`, *non verificabile su questo server* means serving metadata is unknown, not a measured small context; expose valid metadata for the exact configured model. |
| `error` | The probe or metadata query failed, or the declared context is below the required minimum. Read the message: configure tools/schema support, increase the server's active context, or fix the metadata connection as appropriate. |

An `unsupported` or `error` stops the run as `model_capability`. There is no CLI flag to skip
these checks for configured servers. After correcting the server, resume repeats them and
retains the already consumed budget. Raising `--required-context` raises the requirement; it
does not enlarge the server's context. Passing the checks is a minimum compatibility result.
It does not guarantee a successful reconstruction or measure curl performance.

### Read failed attempts

The attempt's `outcome` and `code`, saved in the report/state, distinguish causes:

| Outcome or code | Meaning | Activates local fallback? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `provider_refusal` | The provider declined this logical call. | Only with explicit matching consent, for one additional local attempt. |
| `invalid_schema` | No completed schema-conforming response; this includes returning a schema instead of its JSON instance. | No; check schema/API/client compatibility. |
| `tool_schema_failure` | The agent was stopped after consecutive MCP argument-schema rejections reached `--max-tool-rejections`. This is not a provider refusal. | No; check tool calling, the tool arguments and active context. |
| `context_limit` | The prompt exceeded the available context. | No; fix active context or size the work appropriately. |
| `timeout`, `rate_limit`, `failure` | Process deadline, provider quota/rate limit, or another failure. | No; diagnose the reported cause. |
| `failure` with `network_isolation` | The Codex isolation probe failed. A cached negative probe starts no process and creates no new attempt ID. | No; `--resume-refused` does not bypass it. |
| `not_started` | No agent process was started, for example because the persisted budget or a run stop denied it. | No; resolve the stop/budget first. |

These outcomes differ from the capability report's per-check statuses. For example, a server
whose context cannot be verified is not a provider refusal. Diagnostics and observed rejected
MCP arguments (`tool_rejections`, null when no tool trace is available) help diagnose compatibility;
they do not establish the correctness of generated code.

### Stop repeated MCP argument errors

`--max-tool-rejections N` sets a positive consecutive-error limit, default **8**. The
agent process is interrupted when the native MCP results reach that schema-rejection
streak, rather than waiting for the ordinary process timeout. An MCP result without an
argument-schema error resets the streak; prose and non-MCP tools do not change it.
The outcome is `tool_schema_failure`, with `refused=false` and `output=null`. It does
not activate fallback or contribute to the provider-refusal stop limit.

`REPORT.md` shows the tool name, consecutive streak and total observed rejections;
the result retains `tool_name`, `consecutive_tool_rejections` and `tool_rejections`.
Check the selected model/API's tool-calling support and the server's active context.
Choose a model/API with more reliable tool calling or configure a larger supported
active context when appropriate. Preserve the failed workspace; after
correcting the configuration, a fresh `--out` starts a new run. `--resume-refused` is
for provider refusals and does not recover a tool-schema stop through local fallback.

When the CLI exposes no native MCP results, the report says the rejection monitor is
unavailable and `tool_rejections` is `null`. The consecutive-error monitor cannot
operate on hidden results; `null` is not an observed zero. A self-hosted startup check
also requires native accepted MCP evidence before `mcp_tool` can pass.

### Explicit local recovery after a refusal

Without fallback configuration, Hive records refusals without switching servers. A refused planner
stops planning; a refused worker leaves that module refused. To authorize a local alternative:

```sh
python3 -m hive run --inputs /path/to/approved-inputs --file program --out new-hive-run \
  --fallback-model-server http://127.0.0.1:11434 \
  --fallback-model your-installed-model --fallback-scope role --fallback-role planner
```

`--fallback-model-server` and an explicit `--fallback-scope` provide consent. Claude needs
`--fallback-model`; Codex needs `--fallback-codex-model`; mixed policy needs both. The server
must be loopback and its URL must be the root without `/v1`. The chosen fallback must differ
from the primary client/server/model destination; identical destinations provide no alternative.

| Scope | Selection and activation |
| --- | --- |
| `run` | After the first refusal, all newly starting calls use the local target. |
| `role` | Repeat `--fallback-role` for planner, worker, repair, councillor or tester. Each selected role switches after its own first refusal. |
| `bee` | Repeat `--fallback-bee` with exact logical names, such as `planner-g0001` or `m01-build`; each selected name switches after its refusal. Wildcards are not accepted. |

Only `provider_refusal` activates the switch, for one additional local attempt for that logical
call. Timeouts, rate limits, invalid schemas, context limits and isolation failures do not.
Already active calls finish on their original destination. Hive does not rewrite the prompt or
switch back to cloud after a local failure. Each attempt keeps its own files; the refused
attempt's partial writes are not used as the local retry's starting point. All attempts and
historical refusals remain visible; a successful replacement resolves only that logical work.
Independent council contexts and all acceptance checks remain required.

### Resume a frozen plan and retain the budget

Run the same command with the same `--out` to resume. A verified frozen plan and contract are
loaded without another planner call. Before freezing, validated partial group proposals and
interface decisions are retained. Accepted modules are kept only while their input, assignment,
source, contract, compiled object, compiler policy and review bindings still match. Changed
inputs/maps/planning policy or damaged plan artifacts stop resume; use a new output directory
to make a different plan. Old workspaces without authoritative 0.9.0 state are not silently
accepted as verified resumptions. Do not replace the frozen contract in an existing run.

After a refusal stop, add `--resume-refused` and explicitly configure the local fallback matching
the work to recover. For example, repeat the role-scoped fallback command above with
`--resume-refused` appended. This preserves refusal history and consumed starts. Keep the explicit
local configuration on subsequent resumptions: omitting it after local routing was activated
stops resume rather than restoring cloud routing. Failed isolation probes are not bypassed.

`--max-bees` caps physical agent CLI starts: planners, builders, councillors, repairs, local
alternatives and capability/isolation probes. It does not cap tokens, money or HTTP requests
inside an agent CLI. A new run defaults to **400**; a resume keeps the saved cap when the flag
is absent. Starts interrupted by a crash remain consumed. A budget stop requires an explicit,
sufficiently larger `--max-bees`; rerunning the command does not reset the counter.

Before capability checks, planning and module work, `hive.log` reports a call forecast: probes,
group planners, then
unfinished module builds/reviews, the optional tester and pending probes. Group count is not
module count; interface reconciliation and repairs can add calls. If the minimum exceeds the
remaining allowance, the phase does not start and completed work is retained. The recommended
total adds a **heuristic** reserve of `max(8, ceil(25% of remaining_min))` to spent calls plus
the minimum. That margin is not a completion or time guarantee. Size curl from its plan and
measure the chosen server/model; multiplying lz4's elapsed time is not a reliable forecast.

Keep `.hive/run.json`, `.hive/attempts.jsonl`, the frozen plan and the workspace together.
They retain routing activation, consumed starts, refusal history and provenance. Each bee result
carries `provenance.attempt_id`; `provenance.prior_attempt_ids` preserves earlier attempts of the
same call. If no process started, an attempt ID can be null; Hive does not invent one.
The plan's `planner_attempts` retains those IDs rather than deriving them from model or bee names.

## Safety

- Bees read text that comes from untrusted binaries. No Claude bee has a shell, the web or the
  ability to start other agents (Codex bees differ: see [Bee models](#bee-models)). Each bee runs with Claude Code's `dontAsk` permission mode and file rules
  limited to its own folder (`Read(./**)`, `Write(./**)`, `Edit(./**)`), so reads and writes
  anywhere else are denied; councillors can only read. ReverseAI's MCP tools are read-only and
  never execute the input.
- Each bee's MCP configuration, the frozen contract and the build stage live outside the bee's
  folder or are copied fresh by the queen, so a bee cannot change what the queen compiles or
  checks.
- The original program runs **only** with `--run-original`, in a temporary folder with a short
  timeout and a minimal environment. That is not a sandbox: use it only for software you would
  run anyway, and never for malware.
- Workspaces contain decompiled code and data from the input. Treat them as sensitive.
- Use the hive only on programs you are entitled to analyse and rebuild; see the README's
  responsible-use notice.

## Run it

From the integrated 0.9.0 checkout, with Docker running, the pinned Ghidra image present and
the selected agent CLI configured (subscription login for the default cloud path):

```sh
python3 -m hive run --inputs /path/to/approved-inputs --file program --out new-hive-run --bees 4
python3 -m hive run --inputs /path/to/approved-inputs --file program --out new-hive-run --run-original
```

Run the same command again with the same `--out` to [resume](#resume-a-frozen-plan-and-retain-the-budget).
The queen verifies the frozen plan and saved decisions outside bee folders; module `status.json`
files are informational copies. Inspect the available options with `python3 -m hive run --help`.

## Workspace

| Path | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `survey/map.json` | Functions, calls, strings and imports exported from the prepared project |
| `plan/manifest.json`, `plan/interfaces.json`, `plan/contract.h` or `.hpp` | Verified plan bundle, declarations and assembled interface |
| `plan/groups/`, `plan/interfaces/` | Bounded planner inputs/pages and interface reconciliation work |
| `plan/progress.json`, `plan/policy.json`, `plan/partition.json` | Resumable planning work and the policy/partition bound by the manifest |
| `src/contract.h` or `.hpp` | The frozen interface, read-only |
| `.hive/run.json`, `.hive/attempts.jsonl` | Authoritative run state and attempt journal: counters, routing, refusals and provenance |
| `.hive/attempts/`, `.hive/status/` | Isolated attempt files and queen-owned module decisions |
| `.hive/model-checks.json` | Capability checks for configured self-hosted targets |
| `modules/mNN/` | One builder's folder: `BRIEF.md`, `mNN.c`, `claims.json`, `NOTES.md`, `status.json` |
| `council/` | One read-only seat per councillor and round |
| `build/` | Objects, the linked rebuild in `build/bin/` |
| `check/` | Merged claims and the checker's `verdicts.json` with every re-run report |
| `tests/` | Cases and results, only with `--run-original` |
| `REPORT.md`, `result.json`, `hive.log` | The verdict, its reasons and the timeline |

## Limits

- The bees run on Claude Code (and optionally Codex), so the provider's usage policies and safety
  classifiers apply: work on malware in particular may be refused. The hive recognises a refusal
  and records it in the log and report. Without a successful authorized replacement, a refused
  planner stops planning and a refused builder leaves its module refused. Three unresolved logical
  refusals (`refusal_limit`) stop new bees; historical refusals resolved by local recovery remain
  recorded without counting toward that threshold. Unresolved work prevents acceptance.
- C and C++ output only; Objective-C, Swift, Go and Rust programs are not handled specially.
- The pre-flight recognises common packers and strong signs of obfuscation; it does not unpack,
  and it can miss custom packers or light obfuscation.
- Rebuilt code follows Ghidra's and the agents' reading of the assembly. It is not the original
  source, and conformance cases show equal behaviour only on the cases run.

```

`docs/INSTALL.md`:

```md
# Install and check ReverseAI

Version 0.9.0 installation examples for macOS ARM64 and Linux ARM64. Installing the
Python package enables host-only
analysis on supported POSIX systems. Contained tools additionally require their
exact local images and a separately verified Docker environment. Installation
and `doctor` do not prove containment.

## Requirements

- Python 3.12 or later, with `venv` and pip already available for installation.
  ReverseAI has no Python runtime dependencies; its standard-library PEP 517
  backend requires no downloaded build packages.
- Windows analysis and queries require **CPython 3.12.4 or later** and a new,
  nonexistent output directory for each call. Existing directories, junctions
  and symlinks are refused; older Windows Pythons cannot create the required
  private report directory and refuse output.
- An approved local wheel or a checkout of the desired revision. The wheel
  includes five image locks and the YARA-X ruleset. Image builders, tests and the
  native verifier require a checkout; they are not in the wheel.
- For contained tools: Docker Desktop and the locked Linux ARM64 images already
  present locally. Current native proof covers Linux ARM64 containers on Docker
  Desktop on the Mac. A `py3-none-any` wheel does not establish native-container
  proof on another architecture or OS.

No Node.js, JDK, Ghidra, JADX, LIEF or YARA-X installation is needed on the host.
Those runtimes belong inside worker images. No sample package is installed.

## Install offline

Use a new virtual environment. Run these commands from a trusted checkout or a
directory containing an approved wheel, not from sample contents. Do not add a
package index or upgrade pip as part of this offline path.

On macOS or Linux:

```sh
python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/python -m pip install --no-index --no-deps /approved/reverseai-0.9.0-py3-none-any.whl
.venv/bin/reverseai --version
.venv/bin/reverseai doctor
.venv/bin/reverseai doctor --json
```

Or, from the checkout root, install the source into that environment:

```sh
.venv/bin/python -m pip install --no-index --no-deps .
```

For development in a trusted checkout, use an editable install instead:

```sh
.venv/bin/python -m pip install --no-index --no-deps -e .
```

The editable wheel adds the absolute checkout root to Python's import path;
source changes and checkout image locks are used directly. Keep the checkout
at that path. Reinstall when metadata or entry points change. Never run this
command on a sample directory or an untrusted project: installing a Python
project can execute its build backend. The normal wheel carries fixed lock
copies and does not depend on keeping a checkout.

Use a dedicated virtual environment: the checkout's top-level packages, such as
`tests`, also become importable through the editable install.

On Windows, with CPython 3.12.4 or later installed:

```powershell
py -3.12 -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install --no-index --no-deps C:\approved\reverseai-0.9.0-py3-none-any.whl
.venv\Scripts\reverseai.exe --version
.venv\Scripts\reverseai.exe doctor --json
.venv\Scripts\reverseai.exe analyze C:\approved\file.exe --out C:\reports\new-analysis
.venv\Scripts\reverseai.exe query C:\approved\file.exe --query list_segments --arg limit=16 --out C:\reports\new-query
```

The parent `C:\reports` must exist; `new-analysis` and `new-query` must not.
Windows output is bound to a directory handle until both reports are written,
so the directory cannot be renamed or replaced while bound. Use a different
new directory for every call. Windows handling remains experimental: consult
the receipt for the exact tested host and commit. Use your installed Python
launcher when a different supported version is selected.

The version command prints `reverseai 0.9.0`. `doctor` reports Python, OS and
architecture, lock validity, whether Docker answers its version probe within
10 seconds, and whether each locked image is present. It reads no sample and
never pulls, builds or runs a container. Exit 0 means the host Python requirement
is met; all contained tools can still be unavailable. Inspect the tool rows or
JSON `tools` array, not just the exit code. A present image is not a native proof.

On supported POSIX systems, a host-only query needs no Docker:

```sh
.venv/bin/reverseai query /approved/file --query list_segments --arg limit=16 --out new-query-report
```

Choose your approved input and a new report directory. Reports can contain
sensitive strings and derived text from that input.

## Build distribution artifacts

Build from a clean checkout root using Python 3.12 or later. Check that no local
changes or untracked Python files are present under `reverseai/`: the wheel
includes modules from the working tree, including untracked `.py` files.

```sh
python3 -B tools/reverseai_build.py wheel --out dist
python3 -B tools/reverseai_build.py sdist --out dist
```

This writes `reverseai-0.9.0-py3-none-any.whl` and `reverseai-0.9.0.tar.gz`.
The backend fixes archive ordering, timestamps and modes for reproducible output
from the same tree. Source distributions select tracked files; commit new files
before building a release sdist. Wheels contain application modules, locks,
ruleset and metadata, not image build contexts or tests. The project uses MIT;
the wheel's Metadata-Version 2.4 declares `License-Expression: MIT` and the two
license files, copied under `reverseai-0.9.0.dist-info/licenses/`. The sdist
includes `LICENSE`, `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md` and the same license headers in
`PKG-INFO`. Third-party notices and licenses remain applicable.

## Use local contained images

Each tool loads its lock from `reverseai/_locks/<tool>.json` in an installed
wheel, or `containers/<tool>/image.lock.json` in a checkout. The image ID must
already exist in Docker; analysis uses `--pull never`. Tool flags are
`--with-lief`, `--with-yarax`, `--with-ghidra`, `--with-jadx` and
`--with-jsparser`, where the selected command/query supports them.

The current runtime's snapshot root is `/Users/Shared/rea-safe-staging-501`.
It must already be owned by the calling host user with mode `0700`, and
accessible to Docker Desktop. It is for disposable approved snapshots, not the
workspace or home directory. The installer and `doctor` do not create it, widen
Docker sharing or restart Docker.

Wheel locks are fixed at build time. If an authorized image rebuild updates a
checkout lock, rebuild/reinstall the wheel or reinstall that updated checkout
before expecting the installed command to use it:

```sh
.venv/bin/python -m pip install --no-index --no-deps --force-reinstall .
```

Do not substitute an arbitrary image tag for a pin. Re-run the corresponding
native proof after an image or relevant controller change.

## Approved image inputs and build recipes

Use only artifacts already obtained through the project's approval process.
Builders check pinned hashes before use. They do not run a sample's package
manager or scripts. The common base is
`python:3.12-slim@sha256:16bf2b5c59a08523519d3c8589deca849285dee1d62a3653e124c3dba340f15e`.

| Input | Expected hash in the checkout |
| --- | --- |
| `lief-1.0.0-cp312-abi3-manylinux_2_28_aarch64.whl` | [`containers/lief/image.lock.json`](../containers/lief/image.lock.json): `wheel_sha256`; also pinned in [`requirements.txt`](../containers/lief/requirements.txt). |
| `yara_x-1.21.0-cp38-abi3-manylinux_2_28_aarch64.whl` | [`containers/yarax/image.lock.json`](../containers/yarax/image.lock.json): `wheel_sha256`; also pinned in [`requirements.txt`](../containers/yarax/requirements.txt). |
| `ghidra_12.1.4_PUBLIC_20260921.zip` | [`containers/ghidra/image.lock.json`](../containers/ghidra/image.lock.json): `ghidra_sha256`. |
| `OpenJDK21U-jdk_aarch64_linux_hotspot_21.0.12.1_1.tar.gz` | Ghidra and [JADX locks](../containers/jadx/image.lock.json): `jdk_sha256`. |
| `jadx-1.5.6.zip` | [JADX lock](../containers/jadx/image.lock.json): `jadx_zip_sha256`; its JAR is also checked against `jadx_jar_sha256`. |
| `node-v24.22.1-linux-arm64.tar.xz` | [`containers/jsparser/image.lock.json`](../containers/jsparser/image.lock.json): `node_sha256`. |
| `parser-8.0.4.tgz`, `types-8.0.4.tgz`, `helper-string-parser-8.0.6.tgz`, `helper-validator-identifier-8.0.6.tgz` | [Parser lock](../containers/jsparser/image.lock.json): `babel_parser_integrity`, `babel_types_integrity`, `helper_string_parser_integrity`, `helper_validator_identifier_integrity`. These use SHA-512 SRI, not SHA-256. |

The build scripts contain the same approved input hashes. The locks are the
authoritative values; do not change them to accept a mismatched artifact.

JADX and the parser build offline when the pinned base is already cached and
the approved inputs are present. Replace the directories with your local
approved artifact directories:

```sh
python3 -B tools/build_jadx_image.py --download-dir /approved/jadx-and-jdk
python3 -B tools/build_jsparser_image.py --download-dir /approved/node-and-babel
```

JADX needs its ZIP and the JDK tarball; the parser needs the Node archive and
four Babel archives. These builders refuse a missing base instead of pulling
it, and use network-disabled build steps.

LIEF and YARA-X also build offline from the approved local wheel and cached
pinned base. They inspect that base and refuse if it is absent, never pull, and
use network-disabled build steps. Do not add the optional `--download` flag
under a no-download policy:

```sh
python3 -B tools/build_lief_image.py --wheel-dir /approved/lief-wheel
python3 -B tools/build_yarax_image.py --wheel-dir /approved/yarax-wheel
```

Ghidra's builder still pulls the pinned base and its native-build stage runs
`apt-get` for compiler/make packages. Even with its ZIP and JDK already present,
this recipe needs network:

```sh
python3 -B tools/build_ghidra_image.py --download-dir /approved/ghidra-and-jdk
```

Do not run the Ghidra recipe under a no-download policy. Use the already-built
locked image instead; an offline Ghidra build needs separately approved Debian
packages and is deferred. Installing the Python package, running existing
workers offline and rebuilding images are separate operations.

## Verification and platform scope

`doctor` inspects the environment. The native verifier deliberately creates and
runs trusted control containers to test the profile; it is a separate operation.
From a checkout, with the locked image already present:

```sh
python3 -B tests/verify_m2_runtime.py --tool lief --profile small --offline --lock containers/lief/image.lock.json --receipt new-lief-receipt.json
```

Repeat with `yarax`, `ghidra`, `jadx` or `jsparser`, its lock and a new receipt.
Controls exercise network/write/privilege refusal, PID, memory, wall and output
limits, known answers and cleanup. They parse synthetic fixtures without
executing sample code. See the [security model](SECURITY.md) for the trust limits.

The proven host scope is macOS ARM64 plus a Linux ARM64 container. On the
Mac, run the committed candidate's whole suite:

```sh
python3 -B -m unittest discover -s tests -t . -v
```

The Linux proof requires Docker and the already-cached pinned base. It copies
the selected commit with `git archive`, uses no host mount or network, runs the
suite, builds/installs the wheel offline in a fresh environment and exercises
the installed command on code-built fixture bytes:

```sh
python3 -B tools/linux_proof.py --commit HEAD --receipt new-linux-arm64-receipt.json
```

This host-suite proof is distinct from native worker proof. A receipt applies to
its recorded commit, Python version, architecture and base/image bindings.
Windows remains experimental. No Windows, AMD64 or all-OS containment claim
follows from a host receipt. Consult the receipts for the release you use,
not only an earlier milestone's green result.

## Owner-started host proof workflow

The [manual workflow](../.github/workflows/manual-proof.yml) runs only through
`workflow_dispatch`, after it is on the default branch. The owner selects it
in GitHub Actions, chooses **Run workflow**, and sets `target` to `linux`,
`windows` or `both` (default `linux`). It has no push, pull-request or scheduled
trigger. Do not dispatch it without the owner's instruction.

Each job runs `tools/host_proof.py` on Linux x86-64 or Windows x86-64. It records
the commit, Python/OS/architecture, suite counts, offline wheel installation,
installed version and module path, doctor, and analysis/query of code-built
fixture bytes. The JSON receipt appears after `REVERSEAI-HOST-PROOF ` in the
log and in the GitHub step summary; there is no artifact-upload step. The
package install uses no index, but provisioning a hosted runner and Python is
not an offline operation.

On POSIX, the whole suite gates the host result. On Windows, the real
`tests.test_windows_output` run and installed CLI checks gate it; the whole
suite also runs and its failures/skips are recorded, without being treated as
a successful all-tests Windows proof. A receipt proves only the recorded
checks on that host and commit, not native worker containment or an AMD64
container image. No hosted run is claimed by these instructions.

`docs/MCP.md`:

```md
# Using ReverseAI from an MCP client

`reverseai mcp` lets an AI agent, or any other client of the Model Context Protocol (MCP), ask ReverseAI the same
questions as the command line. Analysis calls run the existing `analyze` or `query` command, with the same checks,
budgets, reviewer and reports. `prepare_file` runs the explicit `prepare` command for cached Ghidra analysis. For the questions themselves see
[USAGE](USAGE.md); for installation see [INSTALL](INSTALL.md); for the trust model see [SECURITY](SECURITY.md).

```sh
reverseai mcp --inputs DIR [--with-lief] [--with-yarax] [--with-ghidra] [--with-jadx] [--with-jsparser]
```

`DIR` is a directory of files you have approved for analysis. The client starts this command itself and talks to it
over its standard input and output; you do not run it by hand.

## What the client can and cannot do

- **Local only.** The server speaks over stdin and stdout and opens no network port.
- **Only files under `DIR`.** Every tool except `list_files` takes a `file` argument: a relative path inside `DIR` (no absolute paths,
  no `..`, no empty parts). A link anywhere along that path is refused, even one that points inside `DIR`, and
  the usual intake checks still apply (one regular file, not a link, at most 64 MiB, unchanged while it is read).
  `list_files` lists regular files under `DIR` with their sizes and never follows links. The check and the read
  are separate steps: another process of the same user could swap a directory in between. As in
  [SECURITY](SECURITY.md), the host account itself is trusted; keep `DIR` writable only by you.
- **Your flags, not the client's.** The contained tools (LIEF, YARA-X, Ghidra, JADX, the JavaScript parser) run only
  when you start the server with their flags and their pinned images are present. No request can enable a tool,
  pass a Docker option, choose an output path or reach a shell.
- **Nothing is executed.** As with the command line, the files are read as data; no sample runs.
- **File text is untrusted.** Reports quote strings, names and decompiled code from the files. Each result begins
  with a line saying so, and the server's instructions tell the agent to treat that text as data, never as
  instructions. A file can still contain text written to mislead an agent, so keep a person in the loop for any
  action an agent proposes after reading a report.
- **Bounded results.** Analysis/query calls default to `view=compact`: reviewed findings and minimal citations,
  without repeated evidence bodies. The text includes the untrusted-data notice and the same compact JSON as
  `structuredContent`; the complete text and the structured content are each bounded to 64 KiB. The JSON is never
  cut, so text-only clients receive the data too; in the text every non-ASCII character is escaped (`\uXXXX`), so
  invisible or bidi characters from a file never reach a model unseen. Use `view=full` to request the
  bounded Markdown/JSON reports (256 KiB text, 1 MiB structured). An oversized report is explicitly omitted; reduce
  the page limit or `max_chars`. Temporary report folders are removed after each call; prepared projects persist
  in the private cache with a copy of the file's bytes until eviction or deletion. See
  [cache retention and deletion](#cache-retention-and-deletion).
- **Errors are messages.** A wrong argument, a refused file, a failed analysis or an exceeded budget comes back as a
  tool result marked as an error with a short, fixed explanation.

## Tools

Tools do not modify approved inputs. Preparation maintains a private cache; it never executes the input. The fixed
catalog is listed in one page:

| Tool | What it does | Needs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `list_files` | Names and sizes of the regular files under `DIR` | - |
| `analyze_file` | The whole-file analysis of one file | LIEF, YARA-X and Ghidra join the run when enabled |
| `prepare_file` | Prepare or reuse a private Ghidra project; returns a small receipt, never the project | `--with-ghidra` |
| `binary_overview`, `list_segments`, `inspect_native_load_image`, `list_names`, `read_bytes`, `list_strings`, `search_strings` | Native file structure, names, bytes and strings, verified on the host | - |
| `list_procedures`, `search_procedures`, `procedure_info`, `procedure_pseudo_code`, `procedure_assembly`, `procedure_callees`, `procedure_callers`, `analyze_function`, `xrefs` | Functions, code and references as Ghidra reads them | `--with-ghidra` |
| `export_function`, `export_program` | One part/page of a prepared function or program | `--with-ghidra` and `prepare_file` first |
| `inspect_android_package`, `search_android_classes`, `inspect_android_class`, `inspect_android_method`, `trace_android_references` | APK and DEX structure verified on the host | `--with-jadx` adds Java to `inspect_android_method` |
| `analyze_javascript_application` | Files, package.json declarations and lexical hints of a JavaScript ZIP, ASAR, npm tarball or bundle | `--with-jsparser` adds the module, call and parse details |

Analysis and query tools also accept `view=compact|full` (default compact); this is an MCP display option, not a query
argument. `prepare_file` accepts only `file`. Each query tool takes `file` plus that query's own arguments, with the types, limits and defaults the command line
uses; the client sees them in the tool's input schema, and unknown arguments are refused. Large lists are paged
with `start` and `limit`, as on the command line. For `analyze_javascript_application` the archive is `file`, and
one file inside it is chosen with `member_file` (the command line's `--arg file=`). A query uses only its own
contained tool: Ghidra for the code queries, JADX for `inspect_android_method`, the parser for the JavaScript
syntax details.

`list_files` returns `structuredContent` `{"files": [{"name": ..., "size": ...}], "truncated": ...}` and a readable
listing. It visits at most 10,000 entries to a depth of 8 and returns at most 1,000 files; names that are not plain
portable relative names (not UTF-8, or with a backslash, a colon or a control character) are skipped. `truncated`
is true whenever a limit was reached or a name was skipped. Analysis/query tools return `structuredContent`
`{"report": ...}`. `prepare_file` returns the bare `reverseai.prepare/1` receipt as `structuredContent`, with
top-level `schema`, `input`, `analysis_id`, `state`, `runtime`, `cache_format`, `artifact_size` and `elapsed_seconds`.
The text includes the same receipt and the untrusted-data notice.

## Prepared native export workflow

With Ghidra enabled by the operator, call `prepare_file({"file":"program"})` once. It can take up to 1,020 seconds,
including lock wait and host work; if the client cannot wait that long, run `reverseai prepare FILE --with-ghidra`
in the terminal first. No analysis call silently starts this warm-up. Existing preview queries still work without it.
Once an input is prepared, its ordinary Ghidra queries also use the prepared analysis.

Then ask for bounded pages:

```json
{"file":"program","part":"functions","start":0,"limit":32}
```

Pass that object to `export_program`, then follow `next_start`. Use `part=calls`, `references` or `strings` for the
other tables. `export_function` selects an entry or exact name and one part (`info` by default); pseudocode uses
`text_start` and `max_chars`, while assembly/call/reference/string parts use `start` and `limit`.
`procedure_pseudo_code` keeps its bounded `mode=preview` default; set `mode=paged` after preparation.

Record the input hash and `analysis_id` with every page. Do not mix different analysis IDs; pseudocode pages must
also share `text_sha256`. A missing/invalid cache entry gives the explicit prepare command. The cache checks every
opaque project's size/hash, while observations still cite the original file bytes; signatures, functions and
relationships remain Ghidra's interpretation. No program export decompiles all functions, compiles code or executes
an input. See [the CLI workflow and limits](USAGE.md#prepared-native-exports).

## Cache retention and deletion

Prepared analyses include a copy of the file's bytes and survive CLI and MCP sessions until least-recently-used
eviction or manual deletion (up to 32 projects / 2 GiB). They remain sensitive even after the original file is removed.
The private folder is `~/Library/Caches/ReverseAI/ghidra/v1` on macOS. On Linux it is
`$XDG_CACHE_HOME/reverseai/ghidra/v1` when that base is absolute and safe, otherwise `~/.cache/reverseai/ghidra/v1`.

To erase the retained analyses, stop ReverseAI instances using the cache and delete that entire `ghidra/v1` folder.
This is also the recovery for a stray file such as `.DS_Store` or a damaged entry that triggers
`Private Ghidra cache is unsafe or unavailable.` Run prepare again to create a fresh private cache and analysis.
An unsafe parent directory still needs its ownership or permissions corrected.

## Configuring a client

The examples use an installed package at `/path/to/.venv` and approved files in `/path/to/approved-inputs`; use
your own absolute paths. On Windows the program is `C:\path\to\.venv\Scripts\reverseai.exe` (Windows support is
experimental; see [INSTALL](INSTALL.md)). To enable a contained tool, add its flag after `--inputs DIR`, for
example `"--with-ghidra"`.

### Claude Code

Add the server for yourself (the default `local` scope, or `--scope user` for every project):

```sh
claude mcp add --transport stdio reverseai -- /path/to/.venv/bin/reverseai mcp --inputs /path/to/approved-inputs
```

The configuration holds your absolute paths, so keep it in your own settings. A project scope (`--scope project`)
writes `.mcp.json` into the project and shares it with everyone who uses it; use it only for paths that are meant to
be shared, never inside the ReverseAI checkout, and keep it out of version control:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "reverseai": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "/path/to/.venv/bin/reverseai",
      "args": ["mcp", "--inputs", "/path/to/approved-inputs"]
    }
  }
}
```

Claude Code asks before it first uses a project's servers from `.mcp.json`. It warns when one tool result passes 10,000 tokens and
stores results over its limit (25,000 tokens by default, or 50,000 characters of text) in a file instead of the
conversation; prefer paged queries, or raise `MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS` before starting Claude Code.

### Codex CLI

```sh
codex mcp add reverseai -- /path/to/.venv/bin/reverseai mcp --inputs /path/to/approved-inputs
```

Or add it to your own `~/.codex/config.toml` (a project's `.codex/config.toml` is shared with the project; keep
private paths out of it):

```toml
[mcp_servers.reverseai]
command = "/path/to/.venv/bin/reverseai"
args = ["mcp", "--inputs", "/path/to/approved-inputs"]
tool_timeout_sec = 1200
```

The example allows 1,200 seconds for a tool call: Ghidra queries can take up to 240 seconds, while prepare has a
1,020-second overall deadline. Use this longer timeout when enabling `--with-ghidra`, or prepare through the CLI
first if your client cannot wait that long.

### Cursor

Put this in `~/.cursor/mcp.json` (your own settings, for every project). A project's `.cursor/mcp.json` is shared
with the project; keep private paths out of it:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "reverseai": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "/path/to/.venv/bin/reverseai",
      "args": ["mcp", "--inputs", "${workspaceFolder}/approved-inputs"]
    }
  }
}
```

Cursor asks for approval before it uses an MCP tool unless your run mode allows it.

## Protocol

The server follows MCP revision `2026-07-28`: each request carries its protocol version and client capabilities in
`params._meta`, and `server/discover` describes the server. Clients that still open with `initialize` (revisions
`2025-11-25`, `2025-06-18` and `2025-03-26`) are served too. Messages are JSON-RPC 2.0, one per line; a line over
1 MiB is refused, and the server never sends requests to the client.

## Trying it without an agent

`tests/mcp_client.py` is a small client used by the end-to-end tests. It starts the server, sends requests and
reads each reply with a timeout and a size limit:

```python
from tests.mcp_client import Client

with Client.reverseai("/path/to/approved-inputs") as client:
    print(client.discover()["result"]["supportedVersions"])
    print(client.call_tool("list_files")["result"]["structuredContent"]["files"])
    reply = client.call_tool("binary_overview", {"file": "sample.bin"})
```

Run it from the repository root with Python 3.12 or later.

`docs/SECURITY.md`:

```md
# Security model

> To report a vulnerability, use GitHub's private form; see
> [Reporting a security problem privately](#reporting-a-security-problem-privately).

ReverseAI performs static analysis of an approved file. It does not execute,
import or evaluate sample code, install sample packages, run their scripts, or
resolve their dependencies. Contained tools parse and decompile bytes as data.
This reduces exposure; it does not make a vulnerable parser or container runtime
safe by definition.

## Trust boundaries

The trusted computing base includes the host controller and its Python standard
library, the gateway, host decoders, claim rules and reviewer, the checked-out or
installed code and locks, Docker and its daemon configuration, and the relevant
kernel and hypervisor. The operator controls the approved input, local images,
staging directory and report destination. Another process with the same host
account can alter these trusted components; same-account staging races are
outside the containment claim.

Sample bytes, archive names, tool replies, and analyst findings are untrusted.
Intake accepts one regular file of at most 64 MiB, rejects symlinks, reparse
points and hard-linked files, checks the opened file's identity and stable
size/timestamps, and hashes its frozen bytes. Parent directories may be links;
intake does not protect an untrusted choice of path or an adversarial parent
directory.

ELF, PE, Mach-O, APK, DEX, ZIP, ASAR, gzip/tar, JSON and lexical-string processing
also occur in the host process. Those parsers are part of the trusted controller,
not protected by the worker's container. An exploit there or a container escape
can cross the intended boundary. No model-provider connection or model-driven
analysis agent is included in the current analysis runtime.

## Report destinations

POSIX reports are created exclusively relative to a bound, empty directory
handle, without following a link or replacing an existing report. On Windows,
each `--out` must name a directory that does not exist. CPython 3.12.4 or later
creates it with a private ACL; older Windows Pythons refuse output.

The Windows binding is designed to prevent the output directory from being
renamed or replaced: it opens the new directory as a handle without delete
sharing, checks that it is empty rather than a reparse point, and keeps it bound
until writing finishes. Each report is created exclusively relative to that
handle with `NtCreateFile`, without reopening the directory by path or following
a report-name reparse point. Existing output directories, junctions and symlinks
are refused by design. These Windows properties await confirmation by the first
owner-started Windows proof receipt. The operator must still choose a trusted
parent directory; these controls do not make a compromised host account safe.

## Installation and manual CI

The package and its build backend are trusted code. An editable install adds
the absolute checkout root to Python's import path and uses that checkout's
locks; anyone who can change it can change the installed program. Never install
a sample project or run its build scripts. The MIT license and preserved
third-party notices describe redistribution terms, not a security attestation.

The hosted workflow is manually dispatched by the owner, with no automatic
push, pull-request or scheduled trigger. It grants only `contents: read`, uses
checkout without persisted credentials, and pins checkout and setup-python to
full commit SHAs. It references no secrets and has no cache, artifact-upload
or deployment step. Changing a pin requires reviewing the actual upstream code;
a SHA binds a version, not its trustworthiness. Hosted runner provisioning is
separate from the offline package-install commands.

Host proof receipts identify a commit, interpreter, OS/architecture and each
check's exit status. They use code-built fixtures, never submitted samples.
On POSIX, a passing receipt requires the whole suite and installed CLI checks.
On Windows, it requires the real Windows report tests and installed CLI checks;
the separate whole-suite result is still recorded but does not gate the
Windows receipt. A passing host receipt is not a successful all-tests Windows
claim or a proof of native tool containment. A workflow definition or an
unstarted manual job is not execution evidence; consult the recorded receipt.

## Contained tools

[`contained.py`](../reverseai/contained.py) builds a fixed command for each
validated operation. Each run uses the local image's immutable SHA-256 ID with
`--pull never`, `--init`, no network, a read-only root, UID/GID `65534:65534`,
all capabilities dropped and `no-new-privileges`. The only host bind mount is
the disposable snapshot directory, read-only at `/snapshot`. There is no Docker
socket, home-directory mount, credential forwarding or caller-supplied entrypoint.
Temporary storage is private tmpfs with `noexec,nosuid,nodev`.

Resources are selected by the operation, not by sample or analyst arguments:

| Tool and operation | PIDs | Memory / memory-swap setting | CPUs | `/tmp` size | Worker wall limit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| LIEF: `lief.headers`, `lief.sections` | 64 | 512 MiB / 512 MiB | 1 | 64 MiB | 45 s |
| YARA-X: `yarax.matches` | 64 | 512 MiB / 512 MiB | 1 | 64 MiB | 45 s |
| Ghidra: `ghidra.analyze`, `ghidra.functions`, `ghidra.function`, `ghidra.xrefs` | 256 | 2 GiB / 2 GiB | 2 | 512 MiB | 240 s |
| JADX: `jadx.method` | 256 | 2 GiB / 2 GiB | 2 | 512 MiB | 120 s |
| JavaScript parser: `jsparser.syntax` | 64 | 2 GiB / 2 GiB | 2 | 64 MiB | 120 s |

Worker stdout is capped at 262,144 bytes. Protocol, input digest, schema,
ordering, bounds and tool-specific anchors must pass host admission before
observations become evidence. A failed run attempts to kill its own named
container and remove its staging directory. A kill error does not replace the
primary failure; staging cleanup failures are reported or attached to it. The
controller does not clean up unrelated containers.

These controls constrain the container. Docker Desktop's VM and its configured
host shares remain separate trust boundaries: a container-to-VM escape may
expose whatever the VM can access. ReverseAI does not change file sharing,
restart Docker or claim a separate dedicated VM around the controller.

## Verified facts and derived interpretations

| Result | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| `supported` | The cited bytes, provenance and registered claim rule support this precise value. It is not proof of execution, intent, safety or absence of malicious behaviour. |
| `derived` | The tool's interpretation is retained with checked citations. Ghidra's functions, decompilation, calls, assembly and references; JADX's Java; and the JavaScript parser's syntax roles remain derived. A byte anchor does not prove the interpretation. |
| `unsupported` | A citation, integrity check, tool registration or claim rule failed. |
| `contradicted` | Otherwise verifiable claims or pages disagree under the applicable comparison rules. Derived or unsupported findings cannot cancel a verified fact. |

The host re-derives LIEF values and YARA-X matches from its own bytes. It checks
Ghidra anchors and referenced strings, binds JADX output to a DEX method's
host-verified instruction span, and re-reads JavaScript literals and callee names
at converted byte offsets. These checks do not make decompilation or syntax
interpretations verified source code, nor prove that a worker found every item.

The reviewer independently recomputes input and excerpt hashes, content-bound
IDs, tool registration and versions, child-artifact bytes and claim-rule results.
Citations resolve within the finding's own result. Archive members are rebuilt
in memory from the approved input, never extracted to sample-selected paths.
For gzip-stream children, the gateway and reviewer precharge each distinct
stream's bound before inflation; failed reviewer inflation remains charged and
cached. Distinct-child and stream budgets are 128 MiB each; each stream is also
limited to 100 times its compressed size, and each child to 32 MiB.

Hashes bind records to bytes; they do not authenticate an upstream publisher or
prove a complete analysis. The reviewer uses trusted host code and is not a
second sandbox or an independent implementation of every parser.

## Verification and known limits

The native verifier, [`tests/verify_m2_runtime.py`](../tests/verify_m2_runtime.py),
inspects the containment configuration and runs fixed negative controls and
known-answer fixtures. Receipts identify image, lock, verifier/executor and
fixture bindings. A passing receipt applies to that platform, image and tested
profile; it is not a general guarantee against escapes or unknown vulnerabilities.
Current native evidence is for Linux ARM64 containers on Docker Desktop on the
Mac. Host unit tests, an offline installation check and a Linux host test do not
substitute for a native containment proof on another platform.

In-process handlers have soft time budgets; they do not have the contained
workers' hard process and memory limits. Bounded parsing can still consume
resources. Lexical hints can match comments or strings and miss indirect forms.
Unsupported formats, paging and observation limits restrict coverage. See the
[contract](contract.md) for each format's limits and the
[README](../README.md) for the user-facing limitations.

Reports contain bounded sample-derived text, including strings, declarations
and decompiled code. Store them as sensitive analysis artifacts; escaping their
Markdown display does not remove confidential content. Upstream artifacts are
pinned and checked by hash, but pinning is not a vulnerability audit.

## Reporting a security problem privately

Please report suspected containment, evidence-integrity or disclosure problems
privately to the repository owner, Stefano D'Agostino, with GitHub's private
vulnerability form: the **Report a vulnerability** button on the repository's
Security tab, or directly
[this link](https://github.com/dagoSte/reverseai/security/advisories/new). Only
the owner and you can read the report. Do not open a public issue about a
vulnerability. See [GitHub's private-reporting guide](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/how-tos/report-and-fix-vulnerabilities/report-privately).
Fixes go into the latest release. No security email or response-time commitment
is published here.

Provide the affected tag or commit, Python/OS/architecture, relevant image and
lock identifiers, expected versus observed behaviour, and a minimal synthetic
reproduction when possible. Remove credentials, personal paths and confidential
sample data. Do not post exploit details or upload the sample to a public issue
or external analysis service. Agree on any sample transfer and disclosure with
the owner first.

`docs/USAGE.md`:

```md
# Using ReverseAI

This guide lists every question ReverseAI can answer, the commands that ask
them, the optional contained tools, and the known limits. For installation see
[INSTALL](INSTALL.md); for the trust model see [SECURITY](SECURITY.md); for an
overview see the [README](../README.md).

## Queries

Ask one question about an approved file without executing it:

```sh
python3 -m reverseai query FILE --query NAME [--arg KEY=VALUE ...] --out DIR [--with-ghidra] [--with-jadx] [--with-jsparser]
```

Host results are verified from the bytes; Ghidra, JADX and JavaScript parser results remain derived readings.
Ghidra queries require `--with-ghidra` and the locally built, pinned image.
`inspect_android_method` adds the method's decompiled Java with `--with-jadx` and the locally
built, pinned JADX image; without it the Java part is absent and the report says so.
Each Java page has a form: `java` (decompiled), `fallback` (JADX's own listing when it could
not decompile), `omitted` (JADX prints no text for the method by design, such as a default
constructor) or `error` (nothing produced).
Pages show `rows a..b of N` and the next `start` (Java pages: `characters a..b of N`); a missing row is never evidence of absence.

| Query | Question | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `binary_overview` | Overview of format, layout, imports and entry point | Verified (host) |
| `list_segments` | Declared segments and their permissions | Verified (host) |
| `inspect_native_load_image` | Segments and declared entry point | Verified (host) |
| `list_names` | Declared symbols, optionally filtered by name | Verified (host) |
| `read_bytes` | A bounded range by file offset or address | Verified (host) |
| `list_strings` | Printable ASCII and UTF-16LE runs | Verified (host) |
| `search_strings` | Printable runs containing literal text | Verified (host) |
| `list_procedures` | File-backed executable functions | Derived (Ghidra) |
| `search_procedures` | Functions whose names contain text | Derived (Ghidra) |
| `procedure_info` | A function selected by entry or exact name | Derived (Ghidra) |
| `procedure_pseudo_code` | Bounded preview, or character pages with `mode=paged` after preparation | Derived (Ghidra) |
| `procedure_assembly` | An instruction page for the selected function | Derived (Ghidra) |
| `procedure_callees` | Functions called by the selected function | Derived (Ghidra) |
| `procedure_callers` | Call sites targeting the selected function | Derived (Ghidra) |
| `analyze_function` | Function info, pseudocode, assembly, calls and references | Derived (Ghidra) |
| `export_function` | One prepared function part: metadata, pseudocode, assembly, calls, references or strings | Derived (Ghidra) |
| `export_program` | A page of prepared functions, calls, references or referenced strings | Derived (Ghidra) |
| `xrefs` | References to the selected address | Derived (Ghidra) |
| `inspect_android_package` | APK members and binary manifest declarations | Verified (host) |
| `search_android_classes` | DEX classes whose descriptors contain the search text | Verified (host) |
| `inspect_android_class` | Metadata and declared methods for the exact class; copy its displayed name | Verified (host) |
| `inspect_android_method` | The class's methods and the selected method's code references; with `--with-jadx`, the method's decompiled Java | Verified (host); Java derived (JADX) |
| `trace_android_references` | References from or to a method, selected by class, name and optional prototype | Verified (host) |
| `analyze_javascript_application` | Files, package.json declarations and lexical hints (`detail` `summary`, `files`, `package` or `hints`); with `--with-jsparser`, module sources, sensitive calls and parse status (`modules`, `calls`, `parse`) | Verified (host); syntax derived (parser) |

## Prepared native exports

With the pinned Ghidra image available, prepare an approved file explicitly, then export bounded pages:

```sh
reverseai prepare /path/to/approved-program --with-ghidra --json
reverseai query /path/to/approved-program --with-ghidra --query export_program --arg part=functions --arg limit=32 --out new-functions-page
reverseai query /path/to/approved-program --with-ghidra --query export_program --arg part=calls --out new-call-page
reverseai query /path/to/approved-program --with-ghidra --query export_function --arg entry=0x401000 --arg part=info --out new-function-info
reverseai query /path/to/approved-program --with-ghidra --query procedure_pseudo_code --arg mode=paged --arg entry=0x401000 --arg text_start=0 --arg max_chars=1024 --out new-pseudocode-page
```

Copy a real entry from the function listing in place of `0x401000`. `export_function` also accepts
`select=name` with an exact `name`; duplicate names select the lowest entry and metadata gives the match count.
Choose one `part`: `info` (default), `pseudocode`, `assembly`, `callees`, `callers`, `references` or `strings`.
Program parts are `functions` (default), `calls`, `references` and `strings`; they never decompile all functions.
Each export query writes normal report.json/report.md into a fresh output folder; it does not write compilable source
files. The prepare command prints a receipt and maintains the private cache.

Follow the displayed `next_start` for row pages and use it as `text_start` for pseudocode. Row limits are 1..128
(default 32); text pages request 64..2048 characters (default 1024) but may be smaller to fit the byte limit.
Pseudocode offsets count Unicode characters after display normalization, not bytes or UTF-16 units. `total` is the
complete bounded decompilation, not the old preview prefix. Keep input hash, `analysis_id` and `text_sha256` while
assembling text; restart if they change. Empty pages and failed decompilation carry explicit status. A truncated or
failed page never proves absence. `analyze_function` and the default `mode=preview` remain bounded previews.

Preparation has a fixed 900-second worker limit and 1,020-second overall deadline, a project limit of 64 MiB and
bounded tables; a large file may exceed these limits. A page does not repeat auto-analysis, but function text still
requires a bounded decompilation in a fresh container. Names, signatures, spans and relationships remain derived;
`library_hint` is currently null. Data references identify addresses, not verified global types: use `read_bytes`
for bounded byte ranges. Preparation and queries never execute the file or rebuilt code.

Projects are opaque on the host and keyed by input hash, exact image, reviewed worker bundle and format. Each
prepared analysis includes a copy of the file's bytes and outlives CLI and MCP sessions until least-recently-used
eviction or manual deletion. The private cache retains up to 32 projects / 2 GiB, including temporary data. Once an
input is prepared, its ordinary Ghidra queries also use that prepared analysis.

On macOS the private folder is `~/Library/Caches/ReverseAI/ghidra/v1`; on Linux it is
